rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.

Lengthen only the gradient to measure how strongly the early critical pair responds to slope. The other pairs have substantial resolution margins, and the last peak should remain close to the 10-minute scoring threshold.

The critical pair improved only modestly with a shallower gradient, so test temperature-driven selectivity while retaining the faster gradient. Raising temperature should also preserve ample margin below the 10-minute time threshold.

Slightly reduce gradient steepness at the favorable temperature to lift the critical pair above R = 1.5. The last peak has ample room to remain below 10 minutes, making a maximum CRF of 1.0 plausible.

The maximum CRF is already secured; now test a shorter method by trimming the gradient window while preserving injection 4’s slope. The higher starting organic fraction should advance elution, while the final fraction remains comfortably above the observed elution window.

Lower the endpoint one grid step to make the gradient slightly shallower and recover the small resolution deficit in the first pair. This should retain a shorter last-peak time than injection 4 while targeting CRF 1.0.

With CRF 1.0 secured, test the unexplored low-temperature selectivity regime: the early pair may separate in the opposite elution order. If it resolves well, that could enable a steeper, shorter fully resolved method.

Test whether a modest temperature increase separates the late cluster while preserving the improved early-pair selectivity seen at 25 C. The steeper gradient also probes a faster alternative to the fully resolved 60 C methods.

Return to the favorable 60 C selectivity and use a slope between injections 3 and 4, targeting just enough early-pair resolution. The trimmed endpoint should still exceed the last peak’s elution composition, potentially delivering full resolution in about 7 minutes.

Slightly steepen injection 9’s gradient to approach the early pair’s resolution limit while shortening the programmed gradient. The final peak may enter the hold briefly, but the endpoint is close to its estimated elution composition, so a long retention delay is unlikely.

The 60 C method now reaches full resolution in under 7 minutes with little early-pair margin. Test a substantially steeper gradient at 25 C to determine whether slope-driven selectivity can break up its late cluster and provide a faster alternative.

Test a higher starting organic fraction in the intermediate-temperature regime to probe selectivity changes that slope alone did not provide. This may balance the early pair against the late cluster while removing time spent below the main elution window.

Lower the starting organic fraction and moderately flatten the gradient to improve the early pair at 35 C. The late cluster was already resolved at this temperature, so this tests an alternative fully resolved operating region while keeping the expected last peak below 10 minutes.

Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 10 while keeping the last peak inside the gradient. This probes whether the fastest fully resolved result can be improved; the first pair is expected to lie very close to R = 1.5.

The faster-method boundary is now bracketed by injections 10 and 14. Test a shallower gradient for greater resolution margin while retaining CRF 1.0; the last peak should remain below 10 minutes, although the third pair may tighten.

Test whether a higher starting fraction can offset the extra time of a shallower gradient while preserving full resolution. This extends the starting-composition search beyond 0.10 at the favorable temperature; injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Preserve injection 13’s gradient slope but lower the starting fraction to improve retention and resolution of the early pair. This targets a fully resolved lower-temperature alternative, with the last peak expected near 9.2 minutes and no time penalty.

Flatten injection 13’s gradient enough to target full resolution of the early pair while preserving the resolved late cluster. The predicted last-peak time is about 9.6 minutes, allowing a maximum-score alternative at lower temperature.

Refine the 0.10-start method with a slope just steeper than injection 6 but shallower than injection 5. This should approach the full-resolution boundary at roughly 7.1 minutes, providing a near-fastest alternative without the final-peak hold seen in injection 10.

With the maximum score and a fast method secured, test a method with more resolution margin. A shallower gradient should strengthen the early pair, while the 0.10 start may keep the third pair separated and the last peak below 10 minutes.

Shorten injection 20’s gradient by one grid step to reduce elution time while retaining its substantial resolution margin. This targets another maximum-score method with more separation margin than the fastest confirmed method, injection 10.

Shorten injection 21 by another grid step, targeting full resolution with the last peak near 7.4 minutes. Its slope remains slightly shallower than injection 19’s, so the critical early pair should retain a small resolution margin.

Back off one endpoint step from injection 14’s slightly under-resolved method. This should restore full resolution with a small margin and keep the last peak inside the gradient near 7.2 minutes; injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Trim injection 4’s gradient window while preserving its slope and favorable temperature, targeting the same full resolution with a shorter programmed gradient. The endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution fraction of 0.56, so all peaks should remain within the gradient.

Trim the endpoint and shorten the programmed gradient relative to injection 6, with a slightly shallower slope to preserve full resolution.
